title: Amazon Q Developer Pricing: Free vs Pro Plans (2026)
summary: Amazon Q Developer pricing offers free and paid tiers. Understand the costs and limits of each plan to pick what works for you.
body_markdown:
## Discover hidden costs and limits on Q Developer


Two limits change your bill: the monthly agentic request cap and the pooled transformation allowance. The $19 seat price is a per-user monthly subscription, while the transformation allowance is counted separately in lines of code.


### Q Developer agentic request limits per month


Each time the assistant takes a multi-step action on your behalf, such as reading files, editing across a project or running a task, it draws from a monthly cap.


A seat price tells you who can log in; the cap tells you how many of those jobs you get.


The AWS pricing page puts the Free cap at about 50 agentic requests a month. Pro is different in kind: it has a much higher per-user limit, and the pricing page lists it as a figure to check at purchase, since AWS adjusts it.


Pro also pools differently from transformation, because the request limit is set per user, not shared across the account.


Here is a worked example. Say your team's typical multi-step task, such as adding a feature across several files, takes about 5 requests once you count the follow-up corrections.


At about 50 requests a month, Free fits roughly 10 such tasks, which is two or three a week. A builder who runs one every working day, around 20 a month, needs about 100 requests and is over the Free cap by the second week.


If your builders lean on agents daily, the cap, not the seat, is the number to divide your workload by.


### Q Developer code transformation limits per account


AWS bills transformation per line of code and pools the allowance across the account instead of giving each person their own.


The[AWS pricing page](https://aws.amazon.com/q/developer/pricing/) lists 1,000 lines of Java transformation per month on the Free tier, which covers a small utility module and not much more.


Start with one Pro seat: it includes 4,000 lines, so a single developer can move a mid-sized service before the meter starts.


Ten Pro seats pool 40,000 lines, which means the team's allowance grows with headcount but everyone shares it, so one big migration can drain what everyone else expected.


Against 40,000 included lines, a 100,000-line upgrade leaves 60,000 lines billed individually beyond the allowance.


Adding seats to cover that is a poor trade, because each seat adds only 4,000 lines.


### Q Developer Pro account and sign-in requirements


You cannot start on Pro from a code editor alone. It runs through an AWS account and sign-in managed with IAM Identity Center, AWS's service for assigning people to applications.


That means a solo builder who only had a code editor installed now needs an AWS account and an identity setup before the first paid seat works.


Budget an admin's afternoon: the cost isn't on the invoice but in the hours, and you should expect the work to repeat each time you add a contractor who needs access.
